title: How India Celebrates Diwali: Five Days of Lamps, Legends and Regional Traditions
excerpt: The main night falls on Sunday, November 8, 2026 — but Diwali is five observances, several legends and a different festival in almost every region of India.
body:
• Diwali's main night in 2026 is Sunday, November 8, when families perform Lakshmi Puja on the Kartik new moon; the festival's five observances run from Dhanteras on Friday, November 6 to Bhai Dooj on Wednesday, November 11.
  • The name comes from the Sanskrit dipavali — a row of lamps — and the clay diya is the one element every regional version shares.
  • The story changes by region: Rama's return to Ayodhya in the north, Krishna's defeat of Narakasura in the south, Kali Puja in Bengal, and a new financial year for businesses in the west.
  • Planning to celebrate in the US? The practical questions — which crackers are legal, where the big public celebrations are — are answered in our linked guides below.

Diwali is not a single day, and it does not tell a single story. The festival of lights takes its name from the Sanskrit dipavali, a row of lamps, and that lamp — a small clay diya filled with oil — is the one constant. Almost everything else, from which deity is honoured to which legend is told to children, varies by region, community and family. In 2026 the main night falls on Sunday, November 8, the new moon of the Hindu month of Kartik, when the lamps are lit on the darkest night of the lunar month.

Five days, five observances

"The festival of lights takes its name from the Sanskrit dipavali , a row of lamps, and that lamp — a small clay diya filled with oil — is the one constant."

The festival opens with Dhanteras on Friday, November 6, a day for buying metal — jewellers and utensil shops record some of their best trade of the year — and for honouring Dhanvantari, the physician of the gods. Naraka Chaturdashi, or Choti Diwali, follows on Saturday, November 7. The third day, Sunday, November 8, is Diwali itself: families gather in the evening for Lakshmi Puja, the worship of the goddess of prosperity, and light rows of diyas. Because of how the lunar dates fall this year, there is a gap day on Monday, November 9, before Govardhan Puja — also called Annakut — on Tuesday, November 10, and Bhai Dooj on Wednesday, November 11, when sisters place a tilak on their brothers' foreheads and brothers pledge protection.

One festival, many stories

The story most often told in northern India comes from the Ramayana: Rama returns to Ayodhya after fourteen years of exile and his victory over Ravana, and the citizens light the city to guide him home. In much of southern India the emphasis falls instead on Krishna defeating the demon Narakasura, which is why the pre-dawn oil bath of Naraka Chaturdashi is the central ritual in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh. In Bengal the same nights belong to Kali, worshipped in her fierce form, and Bengali families also light diyas on long poles to guide the souls of their ancestors. Across western India, Lakshmi is the focus, and businesses close their old account books and open new ones in a ceremony called chopda pujan — making Diwali the practical start of the Gujarati financial year. Kerala is the notable exception, where the festival is not celebrated on a grand scale.

What people actually do

The practice is domestic before it is public. Homes are cleaned thoroughly in the weeks beforehand, on the understanding that Lakshmi does not enter a dirty home. Doorways get rangoli — patterns in coloured powder, rice flour or flower petals — and marigold garlands are strung across lintels. Sweets are made or bought in quantity: ladoo, barfi and jalebi in most regions, karanji and savoury chakli in the west, samosas and malpua in Bihar, and a festive spread called faral in Maharashtra. Gifts and boxes of sweets circulate between neighbours, colleagues and clients, and the retail surge functions in India much as the Christmas quarter does in Europe and North America. On the Varanasi ghats, priests chant prayers as diyas are set afloat on the Ganga.

Celebrating from the diaspora

For Indian families abroad, the same sequence applies on a local calendar: Dhanteras shopping on Friday, the main Lakshmi Puja on Sunday evening, November 8, and Annakut at temples on Tuesday, November 10. If fireworks are part of your plans, check the rules first — our guide to green crackers for Diwali 2026 explains the types, the rules and how to spot a fake.
